Powder Technology

Volume 146, Issue 3, 8 September 2004, Pages 200-205

Investigation of milling characteristics of alumina powders milled with a newly designed vibratory horizontal attritor

Author links open overlay panel, , ,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2004.09.031Get rights and content
Full text access

Abstract

In this study, a vibratory horizontal attritor was designed, constructed and used to produce alumina powders. The effects of process parameters, such as milling time, ball–powder weight ratio (BPR) and rotational speed (RS) of the attritor on the mean particle size and particle size distribution have been investigated. Milling times of 1, 5, 10 and 15 h and ball–powder weight ratios of 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 were considered in the present study. Rotational speeds of the attritor were selected as 500, 700 and 900 rpm and distilled water was used as milling media.
The experimental results show that increasing milling time and ball–powder weight ratio resulted in finer particles. Optimum rotational speed of the attritor was found as 700 rpm. The mean particle size of attrited powders were in the range of 2.05–6.82 μm, depending on process parameters.

Keywords

Alumina powders
Attritor
Ball milling

1. Introduction

The word “attrition” is used as size reduction when powdered materials are being handled. On the other hand, it may mean intentional comminution to bring about a reduction in particle size of a powder [1], [2].
Increasing interest in metal powder with particle sizes that are finer than those of powders produced by atomization has reactivated interest in milling. Milling of materials, whether hard and brittle or soft and ductile, is of prime interest and of economic importance to the powder metallurgy (P/M) industry. Different types of milling methods are used. These include tumbler ball mills, vibratory ball mills, attrition mills, hammer and rod mills, etc. Balls may roll or cascade down the surface of the charge in the tumbler ball mill. In the vibratory ball mill, oscillatory motion of the balls is complicated. The path of the balls and the particles is determined by many factors, including vibrational speed, amplitude, curvature of the sides of mill chamber wall, horizontal chamber of the mill, and charge contact with the upper surface of the mill chamber. Attritor ball mill consists of a rotating horizontal drum half-filled with small steel balls. As the drum rotates, the balls drop on the metal powder that is being grounded; the rate of grinding increases with the speed of rotation. Hammer and rod mills are used in the P/M industry to mill large quantities of sinter cakes, which are intermediate products in the production of metal powders by reduction of their oxides [3], [4], [5].
Ball milling is the metallurgical process of reducing the size of mined ore by grinding the ore in a rotating cylindrical mill containing steel balls of different sizes [2]. Milling by mechanical impaction using hard balls is the standard process to fabricating powders. A jar mill uses a cylindrical jar filled with balls and the material to be milled. As the jar rolls on its side, the balls continuously impact on the materials, crushing it into powder. Milling is not useful for most metals because of their ductility, cold welding and low process efficiency. Brittle materials are more responsive to milling [6], [7], [8]. The attritor is increasingly being used for comminution as it has several advantages, such as operational flexibility, high productivity, moderate energy consumption, small space requirements, ease of operation, etc. Submicron sizes and narrow particle size distribution can be achieved [1], [9]. The specific effect that milling has on a powder depends on the physical and chemical properties of the powder, the vacuum, gaseous or liquid environment in which the operation is conducted, and milling conditions [3]. Selection of the ball-milling conditions, such as the amount of the powder, ball-to-powder weight ratio, ball-milling time and rotational speed (RS) of the jar, affects the properties of the powders produced [10], [11]. Under optimal conditions, the rotational speed of the jar is adjusted for maximum impact velocity. Thus, the rotational speed is kept fast enough to carry the balls to the top of the jar before falling back on the bed of material being ground. Too slow a speed will allow the balls to roll back down the jar side, while too fast a speed will create a large centrifugal force and keep the balls from falling. The optimal rotational speed for a grinding mill varies with the inverse square root of the mill diameter. The volume of balls and input material in the jar should be about half of the jar volume. Metal powders formed by milling are work hardened, irregular and exhibit poor flow and packing characteristics [6], [12], [13].
In this paper, we have presented the results of our recent study on the milling characteristics of alumina powders produced with a newly designed vibratory horizontal attritor.

2. Experimental procedure

In this study, a vibratory horizontal attritor was designed and constructed. The schematic illustration and the details of the experimental apparatus are given in Fig. 1. An electric motor (1 kW) drives the shaft up to 1800 rpm. Energy requirement of the attritor was measured as 840 W h−1. The rotational speed of the attritor was adjusted to 500, 700 and 900 rpm by a belt-drum mechanism. The attritor chamber is placed on four pressure springs. The free length of the pressure spring is 61.5 mm and becomes 51, 41 and 25 mm under loads of 48.5, 95.6 and 156.9 N, respectively. The electric motor drives the shaft and the shaft vibrates the attritor on the pressure springs. The attritor consists of inner and outer shells which are made of Cr–Ni stainless steel. The outer shell is 220 mm in cross-section diameter, 300 mm in length and 5 mm in wall thickness. The inner shell is 110 mm in cross-section diameter, 220 mm in length and 5 mm in wall thickness. The clearance between outer and inner shell is 55 mm. The diameter of the charge orifice is 20 mm and discharging is made by opening the cover of the inner shell. The rotating shaft is 25 mm in diameter, 265 in length and made of Cr–Ni stainless steel. The rotating arms are 10 mm in diameter, 100 mm in length and made of stainless steel. Cooling water was circulated between the outer and inner shells to control the temperature of the attrited samples. The diameter of stainless steel milling balls was 6.35 mm.
In this study, alumina powders were used to investigate the effects of process parameters on the powder morphology, powder size and size distribution. Alumina powders were procured from Eti Holding, Konya, Turkey. According to the producer, the mean diameter of alumina powders was 56.35 μm. Powders were milled for durations of 1, 5, 10 and 15 h in water environment. Experiments were made for 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 ball–powder weight ratios (BPR). Rotational speeds (RS) of the attritor were selected as 500, 700 and 900 rpm.
The particle size and the size distribution of attritor milled powders were determined using Laser diffraction apparatus (Malvern model master sizer) for D10, D50 and D90 calculations. The morphological characterizations of attrited and unattrited powders were determined by scanning electron microscope (SEM).

3. Results and discussion

In this study, the average particle size of attrited alumina powders was in the range of 2.05–6.82 μm depending on process parameters. Fig. 2 shows a SEM micrograph of unattrited powders. As can be seen, the starting powders were spherical and rounded in shape. Fig. 3 gives the morphologies of alumina powders attrited for durations of 1, 5, 10 and 15 h. Examination of powders showed that a platelike structure was obtained for shorter milling time and they become nodular and agglomerated with increasing milling time. The particle size decreases with increasing milling time as expected.
Particle size distributions for durations between 1 and 15 h are given in Fig. 4. All patterns of particle size distributions revealed unimodal type of distribution. After 1 h of attrition, a broader size distribution was obtained and the distribution was shifted towards the larger particle size. However, a more symmetric and relatively closer distribution was observed after 15 h of attrition. Prolonged attrition led to closer particle size distribution as expected.
Fig. 5 shows the curves of cumulative particle size distributions as a function of milling time of 1, 5, 10 and 15 h with 20:1 BPR. The milling time is one of the most important parameters among the others. In addition, it should be realized that the level of contamination increases with the increasing milling time. Therefore, it is desirable that the powder is milled just for the required duration and not any longer. As can be seen from Fig. 5a and b, the mean particle sizes became finer and cumulative particle size distribution curves deviated to the left side with increasing milling time from 1 to 15 h. In the case of 20:1 BPR, 1 h of milling time and 500 rpm RS (Fig. 5a), the mean particle was 6.82 μm. On the other hand, the mean particle sizes were found to be 3.96, 3.23 and 2.98 μm for 5, 10 and 15 h of milling times, respectively. The same effect of milling time on the mean particle size was observed for 900 rpm RS (Fig. 5b). The mean particle sizes were 4.50, 3.10, 3.23 and 2.16 μm for 1, 5, 10 and 15 h of milling times, respectively. These results indicate that the mean particle sizes are decreasing very fast during the first hour of milling in all cases, i.e., from 56.35 to 4.50 μm for 900 rpm.
The effect of the RS on the mean particle size was given in Fig. 6. In this study, the RS of the attritor was selected as 500, 700 and 900 rpm. From Fig. 6, it can be seen that 700 rpm RS resulted in the finest the mean particle size. Under optimal conditions, RS of the attritor is adjusted for maximum impact velocity. The faster the attritor rotates, the higher would be the energy input into the powder. However, there are certain limitations to the maximum speed that could be employed. Above critical speed, the balls will be pinned to the inner walls of the shell and do not fall down to exert any impact force. Therefore, the maximum speed should be just below this critical value so that the balls down from the maximum height to produce the maximum collision energy [14]. Based on this discussion, 700 rpm attritor speed gave the finest mean particle size in this study. The values of the mean particle sizes of 700 rpm attritor speed were 3.16, 2.69, 2.50 and 2.17 μm for 1, 5, 10 and 15 h of milling times, respectively. Some increases in the mean particle sizes can be seen for the 900 rpm attritor speed in comparison with 700 rpm. The values for 900 rpm attritor speed were 4.50, 3.10, 3.23 and 2.16 μm for 1, 5, 10 and 15 h of milling times, respectively. On the other hand, the highest values of the mean particle sizes were obtained for 500 rpm attritor speed. The values obtained were 6.82, 3.96, 3.23 and 2.98 μm for 1, 5, 10 and 15 h of milling time, respectively.
Fig. 7 shows the mean particle size variation of the powder as a function of ball–powder weight ratio. In this study, BPR of 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 were considered. The ratio of the weight of the balls to powder is an important variable in the milling process. The ball–powder weight ratio has a significant effect on the time required to obtain finer particles. The higher the BPR, the shorter is the time required. Since particle formation is through fracture, the smaller the desired particle size, the greater the grinding time and energy. At the higher BPR, because of an increase in the weight proportion of the balls, the number of collisions per unit time increases, and consequently more energy is transferred to the powder particles. But higher BPR may limit the movement of the balls. As can be seen in from Fig. 7, the finest particles were obtained with a 40:1 BPR. The difference in the mean particle sizes for 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 BPR is very small after 5 h and decreases slightly with increasing milling time up to 15 h. As within this study, Moon and Lee [9] investigated the development of nanocrystalline Al–Ti alloy powders for durations of 10, 20, 30, 50, 70 and 100 h in a high-energy ball mill (attritor) rotating at 200 rpm in a hydrogen atmosphere. They found that the mean particle size decreased gradually with increasing milling time until 30 h, then nearly stabilized and steady state was observed with further milling. Similarly, in our study, the effect of BPR was more significant for shorter milling times. The values of the mean particle sizes of 15 h milling time were 2.76, 2.05, 2.17 and 2.08 μm for 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 BPR, respectively. On the other hand, the values for 1 h of milling time obtained were as 5.80, 4.83, 3.16 and 3.28 μm for 5:1, 10:1, 20:1 and 40:1 BPR, respectively. BPR over 40:1 was not studied in this work.

4. Conclusions

In this study, alumina powders were milled by using newly designed vibratory horizontal attritor. In this design, both rotary and vibratory motions were combined. As a consequence, narrow particle size distributions and finer particle sizes were obtained for a given milling time. The effect of milling time, ball–powder weight ratio and rotational speed of the attritor on the mean particle size and particle size distribution of the powders were investigated. The results were as follows:
  • (1)
    The mean particle sizes obtained were in the range of 2.05–6.82 μm, depending on process parameters.
  • (2)
    Unimodal particle size distributions were obtained. The particle size distribution was relatively closer with increasing milling time from 1 to 15 h.
  • (3)
    Increasing milling time resulted in finer mean particle sizes but there was no significant change after 5 h. The mean particle sizes were 2.05 and 4.83 μm for 1 and 15 h of milling times, respectively.
  • (4)
    A 700 rpm rotational speed of the attritor gave the finest mean particle sizes.
  • (5)
    The finest mean particle sizes were obtained with 40:1 ball–powder weight ratio in the studied range.
